proposals.name: Reframes the problem rather than only improving a solution
proposals.instruction: Score how far the abstract supplies a new way of representing or thinking about a known problem, such that the proposed method is a consequence of the reframing. 10 = the abstract states an explicit change of frame (a phenomenon recast in a different formalism, an object re-typed as a different kind of object, a task re-posed) and the method visibly follows from that frame; a reader's mental model of the problem is different after reading. 5 = a modest new viewpoint is asserted but the method would be unchanged if the viewpoint were deleted. 0 = the work is entirely inside an inherited framing (add a module, swap a loss, port an existing method to a new setting) with no change to how the problem is conceived.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high/card-low half is full of frame changes that carry no benchmark scaffolding a criterion bank would catch: R18 casts adversarial defense as a minimax zero-sum game so that a mixed (stochastic) strategy is forced, R52 reinterprets graph convolutions as integral transforms under probability measures which is what licenses Monte Carlo batching, and R48 treats the graph itself as a hyperparameter to be optimized by meta-gradients. By contrast R28 (add a cross-layer attention module) and R49 (swap Euclidean for hyperbolic uncertainty inside an existing self-supervised recipe) are card-high and change no framing.

proposals.name: Names the cause of prior failure and targets it
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states a specific, falsifiable diagnosis of WHY existing approaches fail, and whether the proposal is derived from that diagnosis. 10 = a named mechanism of failure (not merely 'limited' or 'suboptimal'), stated concretely enough to be wrong, with each element of the proposal mapping onto a part of the diagnosis. 5 = a vague gap is identified and loosely addressed. 0 = prior work is described only as insufficient, and the proposal is motivated by its own novelty.
proposals.rationale: R02 says outright that distillation fails on detection for two reasons (foreground/background pixel imbalance; no distillation of pixel relations) and then supplies exactly two matched mechanisms; R53 diagnoses that LOLA agents can exhibit 'arrogant' behaviour directly at odds with convergence and builds SOS off that; R44 argues the cause of adversarial vulnerability is linearity, explicitly against the prevailing nonlinearity/overfitting story. All three are dense-high/card-low, while R20 and R30 present methods with no account of why the incumbent fails and sit card-high.

proposals.name: Load-bearing theory versus appended theory
proposals.instruction: Score whether stated theoretical results are structurally necessary to the contribution. 10 = a theorem or proof is a precondition for the method (the objective, estimator or algorithm could not be written down without it) and the abstract makes that dependency explicit. 5 = theory is a genuine but optional justification. 0 = theory is decorative: a connection 'also studied', a property proved about a component the method does not rely on, an appeal to a framework that plays no role, or no analysis at all where the central claim clearly needs one.
proposals.rationale: R09 proves that the KL divergence between stochastic processes equals the supremum of marginal KLs, and the functional ELBO objective exists only because of that; R27 proves stability and non-dissipativity and derives the two claimed properties (long-range preservation, no vanishing/exploding gradients) from it; R56 proves the search gradient optimizes the same objective as RL-based NAS, which is the whole argument for the method. All are dense-high/card-low. R59, card-high, offers a study of the connection with deep GPs that is appended to a method justified only empirically.

proposals.name: Efficiency gain converted into a new capability
proposals.instruction: Score whether a reported speed, memory or complexity improvement is shown to buy something that was previously not possible. 10 = the abstract states the new capability the gain unlocks (a scale that could not be reached, a quantity that can now be computed exactly, a model class that becomes feasible, a guarantee that becomes obtainable). 5 = a plausible but unstated capability implication. 0 = efficiency is the terminal result, a faster implementation of exactly the same thing, no matter how large the factor.
proposals.rationale: R16 turns a two-to-three orders of magnitude speedup into verifying networks with an order of magnitude more ReLUs and determining an exact adversarial accuracy for the first time; R25 reduces strict-equivariance cost from O(C^2 L^5) to O(C L^3 log L) explicitly so that larger, more expressive models become computationally feasible. Both are dense-high/card-low. R45 (Espresso) reports roughly two orders of magnitude speedup as the end product and is card-high/dense-low, as is R28 with its parameter/FLOP accounting: a criterion bank that credits 'reports efficiency gains' scores these equally with R16.

proposals.name: Regime change versus percentage delta
proposals.instruction: Score the kind of result the headline claim is. 10 = a change in kind: a first exact computation, a bound with a new dependence on a parameter, a complexity moved from exponential to polynomial, a task moved from infeasible to feasible, a phenomenon shown to exist or not exist. 5 = a large but ordinary improvement on an established metric. 0 = a small numeric gain over baselines on standard benchmarks, or an unspecified 'state of the art'.
proposals.rationale: R04 claims the first simultaneous achievement of optimal deployment complexity and optimal d dependence, and R36 moves coreset size from an exponential dependence on (m+k) to O(m + poly(k/eps)) with a near-matching lower bound; both are dense-high with card near the floor (.009, .021). The card-high side is dominated by deltas: R54 reports 10.9% and 12.4% MAE improvements, R28 reports 1.6% top-1. A bank scoring 'reports quantitative improvement' cannot tell these two shapes of result apart.

proposals.name: One governing thesis versus an enumerated deliverable list
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract is organized around a single claim that everything else serves. 10 = one thesis, stated early, with the remaining sentences supplying support, mechanism or scope for it. 5 = a main claim plus loosely attached extras. 0 = an inventory of deliverables ('our contributions are three-fold'; 'First... Then... Finally...'; components i), ii), iii)) in which the items are procedural steps of the pipeline rather than a claim, and no single sentence states what the paper argues.
proposals.rationale: R07 announces three-fold contributions and then enumerates three internal components of its own architecture; R14 walks First/Then/Finally through define-mechanisms, stabilize, experiment; R43 similarly stacks deliverables. All are card-high/dense-low. R08 and R44 are dense-high and each hold to one claim (the last weight layer need not be trained; vulnerability comes from linearity). Enumeration is exactly the shape a criterion bank rewards, because each list item can independently satisfy a separate criterion.

proposals.name: Checkable claims versus promotional intensity
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the paper's persuasion is carried by specifics rather than by evaluative adjectives. 10 = every performance or importance claim is tied to a stated quantity, condition, baseline or scope a reader could check or contest. 5 = a mix of specific and unsupported assertions. 0 = the claims are carried by intensity words -- 'significant superiority', 'remarkable performance gain', 'extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method' -- with no magnitude, no condition and no named comparison.
proposals.rationale: R07 closes on 'the significant superiority of PAPO over baselines', R40 on 'remarkable performance gain' and 'state-of-the-art performance', R13 on 'new state-of-the-art results in HPO' after reciting 12 baselines, 16 search spaces and 86 tasks; all three are card-high/dense-low. R02 (43.9 AP on COCO2017, 4.1 over baseline) and R34 (3 days to 76 minutes, batch size 32868) are dense-high and state what they did. Intensity words plausibly trip a bank criterion for 'demonstrates strong empirical results' while contributing nothing an expert can check.

proposals.name: Motivation names a concrete cost, not popularity
proposals.instruction: Score how the problem is established as worth solving. 10 = the opening names a specific consequence, constraint or failure with real stakes -- a cost that is paid, a threat that is realized, a deployment that breaks -- concrete enough that a reader can picture who is hurt. 5 = a generic but plausible need. 0 = motivation by popularity or open-endedness alone: the area is widely used, is an important open question, is of major interest to researchers and practitioners, has many application scenarios.
proposals.rationale: The card-high side leans on popularity openers: R14 ('Selecting an appropriate optimizer... is of major interest for researchers and practitioners'), R13 ('one of the primary open questions in AI'), R45 ('There are many applications scenarios'). The dense-high side names the cost: R03 describes third-party model poisoning where existing triggers are visible to humans, R22 names the specific gap between real-world perturbations and the narrow sets adversarial defenses actually study. A bank criterion for 'motivates the problem' is satisfied by both; an expert is not.

proposals.name: Subtractive or assumption-overturning central claim
proposals.instruction: Score whether the paper's central claim is that something standard is unnecessary, removable, or wrong. 10 = the headline asserts a subtraction or a reversal (a standard component can be dropped or frozen, a widely held explanation is mistaken, a simpler object suffices) and states it sharply enough that it could be refuted by a single counterexample. 5 = a simplification presented alongside additions. 0 = purely additive: a new component, loss, stage or module bolted onto an existing pipeline, where nothing is claimed to be removable.
proposals.rationale: R08 argues the last weight layer can be fixed rather than learned, R33 argues adversarial supervision alone suffices and makes the perceptual loss superfluous, R26 derives a simpler spectral convolution than its competitors, and R44 explicitly displaces the nonlinearity/overfitting explanation. All four are dense-high/card-low. Subtractive papers are structurally disadvantaged under an additive criterion bank, because they have fewer components to be credited for; R28 and R49 add machinery and are card-high.

proposals.name: Explains why its own method works
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract offers a mechanism for the method's behaviour that is independent of the evidence that it works. 10 = an analysis, identified trade-off, credit-assignment argument, invariance argument or equivalence that would let a reader predict when the method helps and when it should not. 5 = a plausible intuition asserted without development. 0 = the only support offered is that experiments improved.
proposals.rationale: R26 explains that its convolution is a trade-off of low-pass and high-pass filtering, capturing global and local context per node, which is why it resists oversmoothing at depth; R56 argues it assigns credit to structural decisions more efficiently while provably optimizing the RL-NAS objective; R31 unifies existing black-box attacks, shows current methods are optimal in a natural sense, and then identifies gradient priors as the element that escapes that optimality. All are dense-high/card-low. R40 and R20, both card-high, report gains without any account of the source of the gain. This is distinct from A02: A02 concerns the diagnosis of prior work, this concerns the mechanism of one's own method.

proposals.name: Information per word; no restated sentences
proposals.instruction: Score the density of content. 10 = every sentence introduces new content; no sentence restates a previous one in other words; no background the target reader already has; no roadmap or self-summary sentences. 5 = a few padded sentences. 0 = substantial padding -- generic field-level preamble, the contribution re-announced two or three times in different phrasings, sentences whose deletion would remove no information. Judge redundancy, not absolute length: a long abstract with no repeated content scores high.
proposals.rationale: R46 carries dense_pct .996 on three sentences with no benchmark, no numbers and no baselines, every clause substantive; R31 and R48 are similarly compressed and dense-high. R07 and R54, both card-high, restate their contribution repeatedly and open with several sentences of field preamble. Length-insensitive banks reward the padded versions because each restatement gives another criterion something to match, while dense appears to read compression as command of the material.

proposals.name: Contributes a diagnostic or measurement instrument
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work yields a way to measure, test, certify or stress something that others could reuse independently of the proposed system. 10 = a reusable instrument is contributed -- a probe, an evaluation resource, formal desiderata for judging objects of this type, a certificate, a test whose outcome would be informative about methods other than the authors' own. 5 = a bespoke analysis that others could imitate but not reuse. 0 = evaluation is entirely off-the-shelf metrics on standard benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: R11 contributes counterfactually revised documents that both train models and serve as a diagnostic separating spurious from causal sensitivity; R22 formulates desirable properties that measure the quality of any learned perturbation set and proves a conditional VAE satisfies them; R16 yields per-sample robustness certificates and an exact adversarial accuracy; R03 introduces a human inspection test for trigger stealthiness plus behaviour analyses under network inspection. All four are dense-high/card-low, which suggests the bank credits 'evaluates on benchmarks' but not 'creates the means of evaluation'.

proposals.name: Problem encountered in the wild versus constituted by the paper
proposals.instruction: Score whether the problem exists independently of this paper. 10 = the abstract makes clear the problem arises for people who are not writing it, with a concrete setting where it bites. 5 = a real but narrow problem within one research subcommunity. 0 = the problem is defined by the paper so that its method has something to solve ('we study a new problem named X', a novel combination of two existing objectives), with no indication anyone outside faces it.
proposals.rationale: R14 introduces 'a new problem named Optimizer Amalgamation' (combine a pool of teacher optimizers into a student), R32 formally defines learning one-of-many solutions, and R01 defines simultaneous algorithm selection plus metric learning for linkage clustering; all three are card-high with dense at .214, .081 and .013. A bank rewards 'defines a novel problem' as pure novelty. Contrast R34 (BERT pretraining wall-clock, a cost real teams pay) and R23 (replay buffer storage limits in continual learning), both dense-high.

proposals.name: Parity presented as the headline result
proposals.instruction: Score the strength of the headline result on the paper's own main axis. 10 = a strict, stated improvement on the dimension the paper claims to care about, with the comparison named. 5 = improvement on some settings and parity on others, stated honestly. 0 = the strongest claim on the main axis is parity or competitiveness -- 'similar quality to', 'comparable or higher', 'performs competitively', 'is competitive with' -- with genuine improvements only on secondary axes such as interpretability, cost or elegance.
proposals.rationale: R12 claims syntheses of 'similar quality to state-of-the-art models', improving only over older wavelet models; R20 claims 'comparable or higher sample efficiency'; R59 'performs competitively in standard prediction tasks'. All three are card-high relative to dense (.786/.188, .829/.415, .462/.128). Parity phrased positively appears to satisfy criteria asking whether results are strong, while an expert reads it as the paper conceding its main axis.

proposals.name: Takeaway a reader can carry out of the paper
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract leaves a reusable rule, insight or tool that applies beyond the paper's own setting. 10 = a reader working on a different problem could act on it tomorrow (a design rule, a generic recipe, a stated regularity about models or data). 5 = transferable within the same subfield only. 0 = the takeaway is bound to the specific dataset, sensor, domain or pipeline studied, so only workers on that exact task are affected.
proposals.rationale: R44 leaves both an explanation that transfers across architectures and a fast method for generating adversarial examples, and R08 leaves a rule any classifier builder can apply (freeze the last layer, keep the memory and inference wins); both are dense-high/card-low. R05 (Deep Taylor heatmaps for zebrafish swim bouts, artifacts specific to one experimental rig) and R40 (lane-conditioned interaction on nuScenes and Argoverse) are card-high and leave nothing portable, though both are methodologically tidy in the way a per-criterion bank measures.

proposals.name: Sheer elaboration volume of the abstract
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much elaboration the abstract contains: total length, number of sentences, and the amount of subordinate detail packed in (method sub-components, caveats, per-dataset commentary, closing remarks). 0 = a terse abstract of roughly three sentences or fewer that states an idea and one claim; 5 = a standard single-paragraph abstract with setup, method and results; 10 = a very long abstract that walks through motivation, several method components, multiple experimental settings and a wrap-up. Count words, sentences and clauses. This is an extent question about volume only: do not judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the prose is good, or whether the work described is important or thorough.
proposals.rationale: Length is the classic scorecard confound: a criterion bank scored 0-10 per item can only find evidence for a criterion if the text mentions it, so long abstracts collect partial credit across many criteria while terse ones score empty on most. The slice is stratified almost exactly this way. R51 is three sentences with no experiments named, R28, R58 and R34 are similarly compact, and all sit on the dense_high_card_low side; R41, R57, R44 and R18 are among the longest texts here and all sit on the dense_low_card_high side. Word count is not research quality: R51's brevity and R41's exhaustiveness are writing choices, and the same result could be written either way.

proposals.name: Explicit enumerated-contribution scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract is organised with explicit enumeration scaffolding: phrases such as 'our contributions are three-fold', 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ...', numbered problem lists '(1) ... (2) ...', 'Next, ... Finally, we ...', or ordinal signposting of results '1) ... 2) ...'. 0 = continuous prose with no enumeration or ordinal signposting; 5 = one or two signposting phrases; 10 = the body is structured as an explicitly numbered or ordinally signposted list. Score only the presence and density of the scaffolding devices. Do not judge whether the enumerated contributions are substantial, whether the list is accurate, or whether the structure helps the reader.
proposals.rationale: This is a learned template, taught in writing workshops and copied within groups, and it maps a text one-to-one onto the shape of a criterion checklist, so a scorecard finds each criterion pre-labelled for it. R41 states 'Our contributions are three-fold' then First/Next/Finally; R25 runs First/Second/Third/Fourth; R8 numbers '(1) scalability ... (2) interpretability'; R48 numbers its findings '1) ... 2) ...'. All four are dense_low_card_high. R33, R34 and R53 make comparable multi-part claims in unsignposted prose. The scaffolding is a formatting habit, not evidence that more or better work was done.

proposals.name: Density of quantified benchmark results in text
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of concrete quantitative results stated in the abstract: numerals, percentage gains, absolute metric values, benchmark deltas, parameter counts, FLOP counts, speedup factors and named leaderboard figures. 0 = no numbers reported at all; 3 = one vague quantified claim; 6 = two or three precise figures; 10 = many precise figures woven through several sentences. Count how much quantified reporting is present on the surface. Do not judge whether the numbers are large, impressive, credible, correctly obtained or well chosen, and do not reward or penalise the absence of numbers.
proposals.rationale: Reporting style, not result strength: two papers with identical gains differ in whether the abstract quotes them. Abstracts that quote them hand an explicit-criterion bank the literal string it needs for any 'reports empirical improvement' criterion. R13 quotes 1.6% Top-1, 0.16M parameters, 0.07B FLOPs and 3-4% AP; R35 quotes 40%, 0.5%, 2.8%, 43%, 0.8% and 3%; R45 quotes 6.12% and 96.32%; R57 quotes 10.9% and 12.4% - all four are dense_low_card_high. R58, R34 and R51 report no figures at all and sit on the dense_high_card_low side. The presence of a numeral is orthogonal to whether the underlying gain matters.

proposals.name: Inline mathematical and complexity-notation load
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the load of formal mathematical notation carried inline in the abstract: LaTeX symbols and macros, set or space notation, big-O and asymptotic expressions, Greek parameters, subscripted norms, and formal object names standing in for prose descriptions. 0 = plain prose with no notation; 5 = a few symbols or one asymptotic expression; 10 = several symbol-dense sentences that cannot be read without unpacking the notation. Score the amount of notation visible on the surface. Do not judge whether the formalism is correct, necessary, deep, or a sign of rigour, and do not treat plain prose as a deficiency.
proposals.rationale: Notation load is a community dialect (theory venues versus applied ones) and it starves a plain-language criterion bank of scoreable prose: statements of contribution get compressed into symbols that a judge scoring criteria like clarity of method or evidence of evaluation cannot cash out. The two lowest scorecard placements in the slice are the two most notation-dense texts, R50 (R^d, epsilon-coreset, O(m + poly(k eps^-1)), bracketed venue citations) and R56 (O-tilde of d^2H^5/eps^2, linear MDP, feature dimension d, horizon H); R5 (O(C^2L^5), O(CL^4), O(CL^3 log L)) and R30 (l_infinity, l_1) are also dense_high_card_low. R33 and R24 describe comparably technical work in symbol-free prose. Symbol count is a typesetting register, not quality.

proposals.name: Topical centrality versus peripheral or applied subject matter
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how far the abstract's subject matter sits in the field's currently central, heavily populated areas rather than a peripheral topic or an outside application domain. Central markers: adversarial robustness and attacks, large-scale pretraining and transformers, graph neural networks, reinforcement-learning benchmarks, and canonical datasets named in the text (MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, COCO, GLUE, Atari, MuJoCo, nuScenes). Peripheral markers: a specific natural-science or clinical application, an uncommon mathematical object, or a software/engineering artefact with no standard benchmark. 0 = entirely peripheral subject matter; 5 = a central method applied to an unusual domain, or vice versa; 10 = entirely central subject matter on canonical benchmarks. Score topical location only. Do not judge whether the topic is worth working on, whether the domain is important, or whether the paper does it well.
proposals.rationale: Where a paper sits in the field's attention distribution shapes how a reader receives it independently of the work itself. This slice is visibly stratified by topic: the adversarial-and-security cluster R53, R55, R2, R20 and R46 is concentrated on the dense_high_card_low side, while the peripheral entries - R45 on zebrafish swim-bout video, R60 on Ollivier-Ricci curvature for hypergraphs, R40 on wavelet texture synthesis, R47 on a C/CUDA binary-inference library - cluster the other way. Fashion is a property of the audience, not of the research, so it must never be allowed to enter a criterion bank.
proposals.upstream_parent: subfield fashion cycle and the composition of the reader pool the topic draws

proposals.name: Advertised compute scale and experimental-grid breadth
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how strongly the text advertises large computational or experimental resources: very large models, batch sizes or corpora; named accelerator hardware; industrial-scale training runs and wall-clock training records; released pretrained models; and sweeps whose size is stated as a count of baselines, search spaces, datasets, tasks or environments. 0 = no resource footprint is visible in the text; 5 = a standard benchmark suite is run without any scale claim; 10 = the scale of compute or the breadth of the experimental grid is a headline feature of the abstract. Score only the visible resource footprint. Do not judge whether the experiments are well designed, whether the scale is warranted, or whether large-scale work is more valuable.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. The unseen factor is who paid for the GPUs; its textual fingerprint is a scale boast. R23 names a TPUv3 Pod, a batch size of 32868, and a 3-days-to-76-minutes record; R10 advertises '12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks'; R49 reports an Atari 100k score and released models; R52 reports COCO2017 numbers on Faster RCNN101. R51, R28 and R42 have no resource footprint at all. Tagged mixed because a well-resourced group can also genuinely run a more convincing evaluation - the sensitivity band is the honest treatment - but a scorecard criterion asking for thorough evaluation will read budget as merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing group's compute budget and industrial-laboratory backing

proposals.name: Non-idiomatic or unedited English on the surface
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the amount of non-idiomatic or visibly unedited English in the abstract: article and number-agreement slips, calqued or awkward constructions, redundant or circular sentences, unclosed quotation marks and stray punctuation, inconsistent hyphenation, and mixed British/American spelling. 0 = uniformly idiomatic, tightly edited prose; 5 = one or two noticeable slips; 10 = several slips or a persistently awkward register. Score surface language polish only. Do not judge whether the research is good, do not penalise technical difficulty, unfamiliar terminology or heavy notation, and do not infer anything about the authors.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. The unseen factor is editing access; the fingerprint is surface prose polish, which is exactly what a criterion bank containing anything like clarity of writing will pick up wholesale. R59 has 'The most GCNs suffer the performance loss'; R16 has 'we task humans with revise each document'; R20 leaves the quotation in ``noise mode unclosed and mixes registers; R48 closes with the circular 'We corroborate our analysis by confirming the soundness of our findings as foundation of our improved multilingual Transformers', and R12 uses British 'optimised/regularisation' where neighbours use American forms. Editing access is a resource, not a research property, so this is a pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: authors' first language and their access to professional editing or a polishing senior co-author

proposals.name: Group-identifying traces and research-programme continuity cues
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the text carries traces pointing to a particular producing group or an ongoing research programme: repository or project URLs containing a laboratory, group, company or personal handle; a coined, capitalised system name presented as a branded product or as one instalment of a named series; explicit continuation of a prior line of work whose method the abstract treats as its own baseline; framework naming that presupposes an existing user base. 0 = nothing in the text points to any particular group or programme; 5 = a branded system name but no organisational trace; 10 = an organisation is effectively named in the text and the work is framed as the next instalment of its programme. Score the identifiability and continuity cues that are visible in the text. Do not judge whether any group is prestigious, do not judge whether the work is good, and do not attempt to guess or state who the authors are.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Reputation is unseen, but it leaks into the text through URLs and branding. R3 links github.com/locuslab/perturbation_learning; R8 and R43 both link github.com/VITA-Group/... and are both instalments of the same learning-to-optimize programme, with R43 explicitly drawing on 'the field of learning to optimize' that R8 reframes; R57 links ubc-aamodt-group; R23 links tensorflow/addons, an organisational trace of a different kind. R42 and R28 carry no such trace. Tagged mixed because an established programme may also produce genuinely stronger work, but a scorecard must never be allowed to score the letterhead.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing group's reputation and its established, recognisable research programme

proposals.name: Submission-pipeline residue and promissory release language
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the amount of submission-pipeline residue visible in the text: venue form fields pasted into the body (code-of-ethics acknowledgements, one-sentence summaries, keyword or TL;DR lines); promissory or placeholder artefact statements ('code will be released', 'we will publicly release', a dummy repository path) in place of a concrete resolvable link; supplementary-material or video pointers; and mark-up or encoding debris (HTML entities such as >, stray LaTeX macros, mojibake, raw Unicode where the surrounding text uses macros). 0 = clean, self-contained abstract prose with none of these; 5 = one such artefact; 10 = several. Score only the presence and quantity of the residue. Do not judge whether the authors were careless, whether the artefacts will in fact be released, or whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, and specifically a timing factor. Which version of a paper the corpus caught leaves hard textual marks. R48 has the submission form leaking verbatim into the abstract: 'Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge that I and all co-authors ...' followed by 'One-sentence Summary: ...'. R47 links a blinded placeholder, github.com/organization/project, that resolves to nothing. R52 says 'Codes will be released on Github' and R16 says 'We will publicly release both datasets' - both promissory - while R3, R13 and R29 give concrete resolvable links. R35 carries the raw HTML entity 'k>1', and R27 points at a supplementary YouTube video. All of this is pipeline provenance, not research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: the stage and timing of the version captured (initial blinded submission versus camera-ready) and the venue's portal and scraping pipeline

proposals.name: Late-entrant framing versus opening-move framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract reads as a late entrant into an already crowded line of work rather than an opening move in a new one. Late-entrant markers: a recital of several named predecessor methods together with their partial failures; phrases such as 'recent studies', 'existing methods', 'much progress has been made', 'it still remains unclear', 'under-studied'; and an offer to place existing contributions under a common lens, unify them, or amalgamate them. Opening-move markers: introducing a problem, task or object for the first time; 'we formally define', 'this paper initiates the study of', 'we introduce'; and little or no predecessor recital before the contribution. 0 = pure opening move; 5 = a single generic prior-work sentence then a new proposal; 10 = a dense predecessor recital and an explicitly unifying or successor position. Score only the arrival-order framing visible in the text - you cannot see where the item actually fell in the stream - and do not judge whether being early or late, or unifying or founding, is better.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3. The unseen variable is position in the run of entries on a topic, and it leaves a clean fingerprint in how much predecessor recital the opening carries. The slice contains an actual predecessor/successor pair: R37 introduces functional variational BNNs as a first move, and R1 opens by reciting BNNs then noting 'The more recent functional BNNs (fBNNs) address this only partially' - a late-arriving riff on R37 - and the two fall on opposite sides of the disagreement. R29 offers to consider 'the recent and promising contributions in the field under a common theoretical lens'; R43 opens with 'Many analytical optimizers have been proposed ... none can offer a universal advantage'; R7 with 'Recent studies mainly perform topology augmentations ...'. Against these, R22 says 'This paper initiates the study of', R31 says 'we formally define the task', and R53 argues a mechanism with almost no predecessor recital. A dense recital gives an explicit criterion bank abundant positioning material to score, while an opening move offers it none. Tagged mixed because arrival order plausibly also affects genuine quality in both directions - later entrants can be more refined or merely more marginal.
proposals.upstream_parent: the item's arrival order within its topic's entry stream and how crowded that stream had become on arrival

proposals.name: Causal mechanism disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score how explicitly the abstract identifies a causal mechanism for WHY its central phenomenon, method, or failure occurs, rather than merely reporting that it occurs. A 10: names a specific causal factor and traces the causal chain (e.g., 'the primary cause of X is Y, which produces Z'). A 0: reports an outcome or performance delta with no account of underlying cause.
proposals.rationale: R35 argues linear structure is 'the primary cause' of adversarial vulnerability and uses this to explain a previously unexplained cross-architecture fact; R59 derives loss bounds tied to Hessian spectra to explain double descent's mechanism. Both are dense_high_card_low. Contrast R55/R56 (dense_low_card_high), which report numeric deltas with no causal account yet score well on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Resolves a crisply stated open question
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract poses a specific, well-defined open question or gap and then explicitly answers it, versus gesturing at a problem with hedged, speculative language. A 10: names the open question precisely and states a definite answer/resolution. A 0: motivation is vague or hedged ('possibly due to', 'not been shown useful') with no crisp resolution offered.
proposals.rationale: R45 explicitly frames 'it still remains unclear about what graph invariance GCL should capture' and then answers it; R44 states precisely what open complexity question it resolves ('first ... to achieve optimal deployment complexity and optimal d dependence ... at the same time'). Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R01 (dense_low_card_high), which only speculates 'possibly due to the catastrophic consequence' without resolving the question.

proposals.name: Proof-backed guarantee paired with empirical check
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the abstract combines a formally proven guarantee (theorem, convergence proof, stability result) together with empirical validation of that same claim, as a single interacting package. A 10: a specific proof/guarantee is stated AND is empirically tested in the same abstract. A 0: no proof or guarantee is claimed at all, only empirical performance.
proposals.rationale: R11 proves LookAhead converges locally and avoids strict saddles, then shows SOS matches this guarantee while also winning experimentally; R40 proves stability and non-dissipativity for Anti-Symmetric DGN and then validates on graph benchmarks. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R15/R18 (dense_low_card_high), which combine multiple engineering components with no proof of any guarantee.

proposals.name: Verifiable precision of the advance claim
proposals.instruction: Score how checkable and unhedged the abstract's central claim of advance is. A 10: uses precise, falsifiable language ('first to achieve X', 'exact', 'near-optimal', 'certified') that a reader could in principle verify or refute. A 0: uses soft hedges ('comparable or higher', 'may help', 'generally improves') that cannot be pinned down.
proposals.rationale: R44 claims to be 'the first to achieve optimal deployment complexity and optimal d dependence ... at the same time'; R02 claims to determine 'for the first time the exact adversarial accuracy'. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R01 (dense_low_card_high), whose central result is hedged as 'comparable or higher sample efficiency'.

proposals.name: Formal complexity or rate bound as the deliverable
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's core contribution is expressed as a concrete mathematical object — an asymptotic complexity bound, convergence rate, or closed-form equality — rather than only a qualitative or percentage-point claim. A 10: a specific bound/rate/equality is stated as the headline result. A 0: only qualitative or percentage improvements are reported, no formal object.
proposals.rationale: R10 reduces layer complexity from O(C^2L^5) to O(CL^4) and O(CL^3 log L) as its central deliverable; R27 states a coreset size bound O(m + poly(k, eps^-1)) with near-linear construction time. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R55/R56 (dense_low_card_high), whose headline results are percentage-point deltas (e.g., '0.5% average drop', '10.9% improvement') with no formal bound.

proposals.name: Counterintuitive finding foregrounded
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract foregrounds a genuinely surprising or counterintuitive result as its main point, versus reporting an expected, monotonic improvement. A 10: the central claim runs against naive expectation and this tension is made explicit. A 0: the result is the expected direction (a proposed method modestly beats baselines) with nothing surprising highlighted.
proposals.rationale: R09 shows a classifier's last layer can be fixed 'with little or no loss of accuracy', an inversion of the usual assumption that more trainable parameters help; R23 shows attacked graph networks can perform 'worse than a simple baseline that ignores all relational information', a surprising failure magnitude. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R55 (dense_low_card_high), reporting only expected, incremental compression-accuracy tradeoffs.

proposals.name: Conceptual reframing versus additive combination
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's contribution is a single new way of viewing/formulating the problem (a reframing) versus an additive stitch of two or more pre-existing techniques bolted together. A 10: one crisp reformulation (e.g., recasting a mechanism as a different mathematical object) drives the whole contribution. A 0: the method is presented as combining Technique A plus Technique B plus Technique C with no unifying reformulation.
proposals.rationale: R14 reframes the discriminator as a segmentation network, making an entire auxiliary loss 'superfluous'; R28 reframes quantization noise as an l-infinity-bounded perturbation, turning it into a gradient-regularization problem. Both dense_high_card_low, driven by one clean reformulation. Contrast R01 (GA + policy gradient) and R15 (augmentation + hypernetwork), both dense_low_card_high, which read as additive combinations of known components.

proposals.name: Diagnosis of an existing method's failure mode as the contribution
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's central contribution is diagnosing and naming a specific failure mode of prior methods (as opposed to simply presenting a new method that scores higher). A 10: names a specific, previously unrecognized failure behavior of an existing approach and explains it. A 0: no engagement with why prior methods fail; the abstract only claims improved numbers over prior methods.
proposals.rationale: R11 diagnoses that 'LOLA agents can exhibit arrogant behaviour directly at odds with convergence'; R53 shows classifiers 'fail on their counterfactually-revised counterparts and vice versa', diagnosing a spurious-correlation failure mode. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R54/R56 (dense_low_card_high), which report new methods beating baselines with no diagnosis of why the baselines fell short.

proposals.name: Synthesis over enumerative scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score how much the abstract reads as an integrated argument versus a checklist of ordinally-labeled contributions ('First, ... Second, ... Third, ...', 'two-fold', 'three-fold contributions'). A 10: ideas are woven into a continuous argument with no ordinal list scaffolding. A 0: the abstract is structured primarily as an enumerated list of separate contributions/steps.
proposals.rationale: R22 and R26 are short, single-argument abstracts with no enumeration and are dense_high_card_low. Contrast R58, which explicitly enumerates 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...', and R43/R15, which announce 'two-fold' and 'three-fold' contributions — all dense_low_card_high despite (or because of) their checklist structure matching rubric items well.

proposals.name: Evidence efficiency over benchmark-count padding
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's evidence for its claim comes from one or a few decisive, purpose-built tests versus sheer count of datasets/baselines/settings cited as evidence of thoroughness. A 10: a single sharply-targeted experiment (designed specifically to isolate the claim) carries the argument. A 0: the abstract's evidentiary weight rests on listing many datasets/baselines/settings ('12 baselines, 16 search spaces, 86 datasets') without describing what was specifically learned from any one of them.
proposals.rationale: R08 uses one decisive, purpose-built human-inspection test to establish its stealthiness claim and is dense_high_card_low. Contrast R07, which cites '12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks' as its evidentiary base, and R20, which enumerates results across OPUS-100 and WMT as numbered findings — both dense_low_card_high, leaning on breadth rather than a single decisive test.

proposals.name: Generality of the claimed contribution beyond its instantiated domain
proposals.instruction: Score how broadly applicable the abstract claims its core idea to be, beyond the one narrow task/dataset used to demonstrate it. A 10: the contribution is framed as a general tool/framework applicable well beyond the specific domain shown (with the specific domain as one instance). A 0: the contribution is framed as solving one narrow, specific application with no claim of transfer beyond it.
proposals.rationale: R12 develops ORCHID as a 'flexible framework' for curvature on hypergraphs generally, validated across 'synthetic and real-world hypergraphs from different domains'; R57 frames S2GC as generally useful across 'text, node and graph classification'. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R34 (zebrafish swim-bout classification) and R33 (vehicle trajectory prediction), both dense_low_card_high, whose claims stay bound to their specific application domain.

proposals.name: Reproducibility/artifact-logistics signaling independent of intellectual content
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the abstract's content is devoted to logistics/artifact signaling (license terms, binary size, code-of-ethics boilerplate, supplementary video links, exact repository mentions) as opposed to substantive scientific content. A 10: abstract is dense with such logistics markers. A 0: no logistics/artifact markers appear at all; the text is entirely about the scientific content.
proposals.rationale: R05 states its release license, binary size ('less than 400KB'), and GitHub URL; R20 appends a Code-of-Ethics acknowledgment plus a boilerplate one-sentence summary; R25 points readers to a supplementary video. All three are dense_low_card_high — this criterion is proposed in the 'scorecard over-credits' direction: such logistics markers plausibly satisfy a rubric item (e.g., reproducibility) that a dense reader discounts relative to intellectual content.

proposals.name: Order-of-magnitude framing versus incremental percentage-point framing
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract's headline result is framed as a qualitative, order-of-magnitude leap (multiplicative speedups, categorical capability jumps) versus an incremental percentage-point delta. A 10: headline number is a multiplicative/order-of-magnitude claim (e.g., 'two to three orders of magnitude', 'from 3 days to 76 minutes'). A 0: headline number is a single-digit percentage-point delta with no larger framing.
proposals.rationale: R02 reports its verifier is 'two to three orders of magnitude quicker than the state-of-the-art'; R46 reduces BERT training 'from 3 days to just 76 minutes'. Both dense_high_card_low. Contrast R55/R56 (dense_low_card_high), whose headline numbers are percentage-point deltas ('0.5% average drop', '10.9% and 12.4% improvement').

proposals.name: Elegance via removal rather than addition
proposals.instruction: Score whether the method achieves its result by removing, freezing, or simplifying an existing component (fewer moving parts than the prior standard approach) versus by adding new auxiliary machinery on top of an existing pipeline. A 10: the abstract's central move is eliminating/fixing/simplifying a component while maintaining or improving performance. A 0: the central move is stacking additional modules/losses/mechanisms onto an existing pipeline.
proposals.rationale: R09 fixes the classifier's last layer (removing trainable parameters) with 'little or no loss of accuracy'; R14 removes the VGG-based perceptual loss entirely, making it 'superfluous'. Both dense_high_card_low, both wins-via-subtraction. Contrast R15 (adds a hypernetwork plus population-size encoding on top of standard policy optimization) and R18 (adds hyperbolic uncertainty weighting on top of self-supervised learning), both dense_low_card_high, both wins-via-addition.

proposals.name: Cross-disciplinary borrowing used to derive a result, not just to survey one
proposals.instruction: Score whether a concept imported from a distant field (game theory, optimal transport, causality, information theory, algebraic topology) is used to derive or prove a specific new result, versus being used only to organize or survey existing techniques under a shared vocabulary. A 10: the outside-field concept is the engine of a specific new proof, bound, or mechanism. A 0: the outside-field concept is invoked only to provide a descriptive overview or taxonomy of existing methods, with no new result derived from it.
proposals.rationale: R16 imports minimax game theory to derive a specific mixed-strategy defense (Stochastic Activation Pruning) with a concrete mechanism; R12 imports optimal-transport-flavored Ollivier-Ricci curvature and proves new theoretical properties for hypergraphs. Both dense_high_card_low, both using the import to derive something new. Contrast R51 (dense_low_card_high), which imports algebraic topology mainly to give a 'self-contained overview' and 'intuitive guidance' for designing losses, without deriving a comparably sharp new proof.

proposals.name: Numeric-result density in the abstract text
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale (0 = no concrete numbers anywhere; 10 = numbers embedded in nearly every sentence), rate how densely the abstract is packed with specific numeric claims -- percentages, factor-of-N speedups, counts, hyperparameter values, timings, benchmark scores. Score only how much quantified detail is present in the text; do NOT judge whether the reported numbers are impressive, correct, or indicative of genuine quality.
proposals.rationale: R09 saturates its abstract with quantified claims ('76 minutes', batch size '32868', 'TPUv3 Pod', 'reduced from 3 days') and R36 does the same ('10.9% and 12.4% improvement'), on opposite sides of the disagreement slice. Raw quantifier density is available to any reader or scorecard criterion independent of whether the underlying numbers reflect a real advance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (sales-pitch writing habit)

proposals.name: Self-descriptive or playfully branded title/method naming
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate the extent to which the paper's title or coined method name uses playful branding, self-descriptive/self-congratulatory language, or a snappy constructed acronym, as opposed to a plain descriptive title. Score only how much branding/marketing framing is present in the naming; do NOT judge whether the branding is deserved or whether the underlying method is good.
proposals.rationale: R08's title literally contains the self-congratulatory phrase 'A Very Good Method', and R43 packages its contribution as the catchy constructed acronym 'SNAS'. Both are naming-level marketing moves a reader could respond to independent of the work's substance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (marketing/branding savvy)

proposals.name: Abstract length and verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale (0 = extremely terse, about 2-3 sentences; 10 = unusually long and exhaustively enumerated), rate how long and verbose the abstract text is relative to a typical one-paragraph abstract. Score only length/verbosity; do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the content itself is good.
proposals.rationale: R51 is by far the longest, most exhaustively enumerated abstract in the slice, while R47 is only three sentences with no results discussion at all. Raw verbosity is scorable without touching substance and could differentially favor whichever model rewards apparent thoroughness or penalizes terseness.

proposals.name: Code/data repository link or release-promise presence
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale (0 = no pointer to shareable artifacts anywhere; 10 = an explicit repository URL plus explicit release/licensing language), rate how prominently the text contains a pointer to code or data availability -- a URL, or an explicit sentence promising future release. Score only whether/how prominently such a pointer appears; do NOT judge whether the released artifact would actually be useful or complete.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R36 (both dense_low_card_high) each close with an explicit GitHub URL for code release, a pattern that recurs roughly three times more often on the card-favored side of this slice than on the dense-favored side (e.g. R01 and R03 carry no such link). This reproducibility-signaling habit is not the research quality itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format / lab's open-science norm

proposals.name: Named large-scale computing infrastructure or hardware mentions
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text names specific large-scale or branded computing infrastructure, hardware, or vendor platforms (e.g. a named cloud TPU/GPU pod, a named trusted-hardware enclave, a named corporate code namespace) as part of describing the experiments. Score only the presence/specificity of such named infrastructure mentions; do NOT judge whether that infrastructure was necessary or whether the resulting research is good.
proposals.rationale: R09 names Google's 'TPUv3 Pod', and R34 names 'Intel SGX' and 'Sanctum' as specific hardware platforms. Citing named, branded infrastructure is a textual trace of which labs had access to particular resources, independent of whether the resulting science is good.

proposals.name: Non-narrative trailing paratext (ethics/summary tags, media links)
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much of the text is occupied by content that sits outside the core scientific narrative -- e.g. leftover submission-form fields (ethics-statement acknowledgments, one-sentence-summary tags), or pointers to supplementary media such as a video link -- appended after or alongside the technical description. Score only the presence/amount of such appended non-narrative material; do NOT judge whether that material is appropriate or well produced.
proposals.rationale: R51 carries visible leftover submission-portal fields ('Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge that I and all co-authors...', 'One-sentence Summary: ...') stitched onto the end of the abstract, and R22 appends a supplementary video pointer ('We encourage readers to view a supplementary video ... summarizing our results'). Both are artifacts of how completely, and from where in the pipeline, the item's text was captured -- not of the work's merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics on the receiving side (submission-portal form-field bleed-through)

proposals.name: Field-commentary rhetorical framing before the technical contribution
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text opens with meta-commentary about the state of the field, a debate, or a pedagogical/expository framing move before stating its own technical contribution, as opposed to jumping straight into the method. Score only the presence of this rhetorical framing move; do NOT judge whether the framing is insightful or whether the paper itself is good.
proposals.rationale: R32 opens with a meta-commentary move ('the term lacks coherent meaning in standard statistical frameworks. However, the language of causality offers clarity') before stating its contribution, and R60 adopts an explicit pedagogical register ('We include a self-contained overview of the required foundational concepts ... and provide intuitive guidance'). This field-level rhetorical framing is a writing-practice fingerprint, not a quality signal by itself.

proposals.name: Fashionable ML buzzword topicality density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how densely the text is packed with currently-fashionable machine-learning buzzwords and topic labels (e.g. terms naming trending architectures, paradigms, or subfields), as opposed to plain, classical, or niche terminology. Score only the density of fashionable topic-labeling language; do NOT judge whether the topic choice itself is good research.
proposals.rationale: R56 stacks currently-fashionable terms ('Transformers', 'world models', sample-efficient reinforcement learning), and R11 similarly stacks fashionable terms ('graph contrastive learning', 'self-supervised learning', spectral augmentation). Topical bandwagon language marks when/what was trending at submission time rather than the work's quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: timing of submission relative to what topics are fashionable in the field

proposals.name: Named-predecessor differentiation density (crowded-subfield lateness signal)
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text explicitly names and differentiates itself from specific prior methods or algorithms by name/acronym (e.g. 'unlike X', 'compared to Y'), as opposed to staking out a problem without naming any specific predecessor technique. Score only the density of named-predecessor engagement; do NOT judge whether the differentiation is fair or whether the paper is actually better than what it names.
proposals.rationale: R09 explicitly names and positions against a specific predecessor ('LARS ... performs poorly for attention models like BERT'), and R52 explicitly unifies and differentiates itself from several named prior techniques ('convex potential layers', 'Almost-Orthogonal-Layer'). Dense engagement with named predecessors is a trace of how late/crowded the surrounding topic-stream already was at the time of writing, not of the item's own quality -- an item entering a mature, crowded thread reads very differently from one staking out an early, uncontested problem.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / topic-maturity timing at time of writing

proposals.name: Scare-quote/jargon-flagging punctuation habit
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how often the text uses quotation marks (straight or paired backtick-style) to flag a coined term or jargon phrase as noteworthy, as opposed to writing all terms unmarked. Score only the frequency of this quoting habit; do NOT judge whether the flagged terms are well-chosen or whether the paper's content is good.
proposals.rationale: R12 flags its central term with paired quote marks ('Double descent' delineates...), and R35 similarly sets off a coined term in quotes (the ''noise mode.''). This orthographic habit of visually flagging jargon is a typographic tic scorable without reading for substance.

proposals.name: Theory-to-mechanism alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed mechanism directly follows from a precise theoretical diagnosis of the stated problem; score 0 when theory and mechanism are disconnected or merely juxtaposed.
proposals.rationale: R01, R09, and R24 tightly connect formal analysis to the proposed algorithm, unlike abstracts whose theory is mainly decorative.

proposals.name: Bottleneck-specific intervention
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure bottleneck and introduces a narrowly targeted remedy for it; score 0 when the method is generic or the bottleneck is vague.
proposals.rationale: R03, R05, and R55 each isolate a specific obstacle and design the method around that obstacle.

proposals.name: Constraint-preserving innovation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method improves a capability while explicitly preserving important constraints such as privacy, deployment limits, data scarcity, or compatibility; score 0 when it improves one dimension by ignoring the others.
proposals.rationale: R03, R24, and R26 demonstrate innovation under deployment, quantization, or privacy constraints rather than unconstrained optimization.

proposals.name: Unification that generates novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a common formal perspective genuinely subsumes prior approaches and produces new methods or predictions; score 0 when “unification” is only a relabeling of existing techniques.
proposals.rationale: R39, R49, and R50 use a shared mathematical perspective to derive broader architectures or quantities.

proposals.name: Causal failure diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies why an established approach fails, supports that diagnosis with a controlled example or analysis, and derives a remedy; score 0 when it only reports failure or improvement.
proposals.rationale: R11, R23, and R53 connect observed failures to specific causes and use those causes to motivate corrective methods.

proposals.name: Adversarial coverage realism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when robustness is evaluated against perturbations that vary in structure, visibility, access, or transferability and the method addresses those dimensions; score 0 when robustness is shown only for one convenient attack.
proposals.rationale: R06, R27, and R43 consider stealth, limited attacker knowledge, graph manipulation, or realistic perturbation families.

proposals.name: Problem-structure inductive fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the architecture or objective encodes a structural property intrinsic to the problem and explains why that property should help; score 0 when the design is architecture-agnostic without a problem-specific rationale.
proposals.rationale: R17, R21, and R55 align spectral, semantic, or relational structure with the learning objective.

proposals.name: Compositional reuse across settings
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one learned component is explicitly reusable across tasks, scales, policies, domains, or input conditions with a clear composition mechanism; score 0 when each setting requires a separate bespoke solution.
proposals.rationale: R05, R18, and R19 emphasize transition, population-size, or motor-policy reuse across related settings.

proposals.name: Operational resource accounting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when computational, memory, sample, or deployment savings are quantified together with the mechanism and operating conditions that produce them; score 0 when efficiency is asserted only with vague adjectives.
proposals.rationale: R20, R32, and R39 give concrete complexity, hardware, or throughput mechanisms rather than generic efficiency claims.

proposals.name: Claim-matched evaluation breadth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation spans the datasets, architectures, tasks, baselines, and stress conditions implied by the claims; score 0 when broad claims rest on a narrow or mismatched experiment.
proposals.rationale: R07, R36, and R49 pair wide experimental coverage with claims about general utility or robustness.

proposals.name: Failure-aware uncertainty modeling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty is modeled at the level where the abstract identifies uncertainty arising, and evaluation tests reliability or calibration consequences; score 0 when uncertainty is added without a failure model or reliability check.
proposals.rationale: R11, R15, and R31 connect uncertainty representations to optimizer pathologies, predictive reliability, or decision-time exploration.

proposals.name: Distribution-shift and counterfactual discipline
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly distinguishes in-distribution behavior from shifted, counterfactual, or unseen conditions and evaluates that distinction; score 0 when generalization is inferred only from ordinary held-out data.
proposals.rationale: R35, R43, and R53 directly construct or study altered conditions to test whether learned behavior survives distributional change.

proposals.name: Multiplicity-aware prediction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method represents multiple valid, plausible, or future solutions and explains how training avoids collapsing them improperly; score 0 when inherently multimodal outputs are forced into one undifferentiated prediction.
proposals.rationale: R16, R19, and R58 explicitly address multiple solutions, behaviors, or future interactions.

proposals.name: Interpretability with intervention
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when analysis reveals what the model uses and that insight leads to a concrete intervention, correction, or design choice; score 0 when interpretability is limited to visualization without explanatory or corrective use.
proposals.rationale: R23, R48, and R49 connect interpretability or algebraic transparency to artifact removal, symbolic rules, or design generalization.

proposals.name: Assumption-to-guarantee calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when theoretical or empirical guarantees are stated with precise assumptions, scope, and limitations that match the proposed setting; score 0 when sweeping guarantees are made without specifying their conditions.
proposals.rationale: R01, R03, and R37 carefully state convergence, sample-complexity, or verification claims with explicit problem conditions.

proposals.name: Named-method branding density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses named methods, catchy acronyms, or branded project labels; judge presence only, not whether the naming is good or reflects research quality.
proposals.rationale: Distinctive labels can make an abstract more memorable to text models without indicating research quality. Examples include ORCHID and PAPO in R02 and R06, and SLL and MRLA in R07 and R46.

proposals.name: Artifact-release signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains code links, licenses, released models, supplementary media, or reproducibility statements; judge extent only, not whether the artifacts are useful or the work is high quality.
proposals.rationale: Artifact-release habits can leave highly visible textual markers that affect model responses independently of the underlying contribution. R04 mentions a license and repository, while R35 mentions a supplementary video and R38 gives an implementation link.

proposals.name: Quantified-result density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how densely the text presents percentages, multipliers, time reductions, benchmark scores, parameter counts, or other numerical outcomes; judge amount only, not whether the numbers are impressive or credible.
proposals.rationale: Numerical specificity can function as a persuasive textual cue without itself being research quality. R21 contains several percentage improvements, while R38 combines a 76-minute claim, batch size, and multi-day comparison; R40 gives detailed percentages and distortion values.

proposals.name: Contribution-template density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract follows an explicit contribution template using ordered claims such as first, second, third, finally, we propose, we show, and we evaluate; judge stylistic extent only, not whether the contributions are good.
proposals.rationale: Template-like sequencing can be learned as a genre cue even when it says nothing by itself about research quality. R06 explicitly enumerates three contributions, and R08 uses a first-through-fourth progression of claims.

proposals.name: Reference and proper-name density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains named prior methods, researchers, datasets, benchmarks, architectures, venues, or application domains; judge textual abundance only, not the relevance or correctness of the references.
proposals.rationale: Dense naming may reflect an author's scholarly community, field conventions, or audience targeting, all of which can influence text-based responses while only indirectly relating to quality. R07 names several prior approaches and mathematical tools, while R25 names multiple detector families and COCO2017.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's field familiarity and venue-positioning practice

proposals.name: Formalism and theorem density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses equations, asymptotic notation, named theorems, proofs, bounds, optimization conditions, or other formal mathematical language; judge amount only, not whether the formalism is rigorous or valuable.
proposals.rationale: Theoretical communities leave recognizable mathematical fingerprints that can affect model behavior and may also correlate with genuine expertise. R16 uses coreset bounds and epsilon notation, while R32 uses deployment-complexity formulas, lower bounds, and experiment-design terminology.

proposals.name: Evaluation-breadth signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text lists many datasets, tasks, domains, architectures, baselines, or experimental settings; judge the breadth of enumeration only, not whether the evaluation is adequate or persuasive.
proposals.rationale: Broad evaluation inventories can be expected by particular venues or communities and can attract text-model attention independently of the strength of any individual result. R27 lists spherical benchmark settings and model variants, while R39 spans transformations, corruptions, lighting, robustness, and generalization.

proposals.name: Systems and deployment framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text emphasizes runtime, memory, hardware, throughput, scalability, implementation constraints, or deployment settings; judge presence only, not whether the system is useful or well engineered.
proposals.rationale: Engineering and deployment language can be salient to models because it resembles practical impact writing, while the framing itself is not research quality. R04 emphasizes binary files, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and speed, while R48 emphasizes TEEs, processors, throughput, and inference.
proposals.upstream_parent: application-facing lab practice or deployment-oriented audience

proposals.name: Safety and security framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses security, adversarial, trust, privacy, reliability, threat, or safety-oriented framing; judge topical presence only, not whether the concern is important or the work is responsible.
proposals.rationale: Security-oriented vocabulary can be a fashionable domain marker that changes textual reception without establishing research quality. R03 repeatedly invokes threats, stealthiness, and defenses, while R60 uses adversaries, robustness, reliability, and calibration language.

proposals.name: Container-position rhetoric
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract reads as a prompt-literal, obvious treatment versus a late-arriving reframing that emphasizes a neglected angle, contrast, synthesis, or exception; judge only the textual style, not whether the framing is good.
proposals.rationale: If obvious approaches had already appeared in the stream, later writers might leave contrastive or reframing fingerprints; prior exposure and extra editing time could also affect genuine writing quality. R23 presents a direct alternative explanation centered on linearity, whereas R56 explicitly reframes spuriousness through causality and counterfactual revision.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and exposure to earlier entries

proposals.name: Failure-mechanism alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mechanism and the intervention directly changes that mechanism; score 0 when the method is presented without a mechanism-level link to the stated problem.
proposals.rationale: R04 links stochastic pruning to mixed strategies against adversaries; R47 links its distillation design to foreground imbalance and missing pixel relations; R50 links sampling regularization to background oversampling.

proposals.name: Falsifiable explanatory insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the paper proposes a non-obvious explanation that yields testable predictions or quantitative consequences; score 0 when it only introduces a method and reports aggregate improvements.
proposals.rationale: R09 explains adversarial vulnerability through linearity; R34 derives graph behavior from spectral filtering; R51 connects double descent to loss functions and Hessian spectra.

proposals.name: Theory-to-design continuity

proposals.name: Explanatory accessibility style

proposals.name: Late-riff positioning cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract reads linguistically like a follow-on, synthesis, rebuttal, or reframing of obvious prior approaches, using cues such as 'towards,' 'unified,' 'further,' 'instead,' or 'meets'; do not judge whether the framing is good.
proposals.rationale: R05 presents a unifying extension, R21 reframes an established concern, and R54 explicitly unifies existing approaches; R60 also combines familiar components. proposals.name: Problem Reframing Power
proposals.instruction: Score how much the abstract reconceptualizes a known problem in a fundamentally new light, making the solution path natural or obvious. 10 = the paper changes how the community will think about the problem (e.g., identifying a previously unnoticed cause or reframing the objective); 0 = the problem is stated and attacked exactly as in prior work with no new perspective.

proposals.name: Core Insight Economy
proposals.instruction: Score whether the contribution is one simple, powerful idea whose impact is disproportionate to its complexity. 10 = a single, easily stated insight that explains or enables much; 0 = a complex system of many moving parts with no single unifying idea that could be transmitted in one sentence.

proposals.name: Provable Near-Optimality with Matching Bounds
proposals.instruction: Score whether the paper provides formal guarantees of optimality or near-optimality, ideally with matching lower bounds showing the guarantee is tight. 10 = proved near-optimal with a matching lower bound demonstrating tightness; 5 = a non-trivial upper bound or convergence proof without a matching lower bound; 0 = no formal complexity or optimality guarantee.
