proposals.name: Novel Mathematical Construct Introduced
proposals.instruction: Score whether the paper introduces a genuinely new mathematical object, operator, or formalism not previously seen in the literature. 10 = a first-of-kind mathematical object (new layer type, new invariant, new distance measure) with defined properties; 0 = uses only standard, well-known mathematical constructs.
proposals.rationale: R48 introduces the 2-simplicial Transformer with higher-dimensional attention using tensor products of value vectors—a genuinely new construct. R17 introduces ORCHID, generalizing Ollivier-Ricci curvature to hypergraphs. R18 defines a functional ELBO directly on stochastic processes. These are mathematical innovations, not just engineering improvements, and the dense model appears to reward them heavily.

proposals.name: Counterintuitive Discovery
proposals.instruction: Score how surprising the central finding is relative to what the community would expect. 10 = the result contradicts widely held beliefs or the obvious intuition; 5 = mildly surprising; 0 = confirms what most researchers would have predicted.
proposals.rationale: R26 shows attacks can make GNNs perform worse than a baseline ignoring all relational information—deeply surprising. R34 reveals that linearity (not complexity) causes adversarial vulnerability, contradicting the prevailing nonlinearity hypothesis. R46 shows that adversarial supervision alone can match perceptual-loss-trained GANs. Dense_low items like R05 (Transformers work well) and R39 (more layer interaction helps) are more predictable.

proposals.name: Transformative Practical Magnitude
proposals.instruction: Score the qualitative scale of practical improvement reported. 10 = orders-of-magnitude speedup, or enabling something previously impossible; 5 = substantial percentage-point gains; 0 = marginal or incomparable improvements.
proposals.rationale: R33 achieves 2-3 orders of magnitude speedup in verification and determines exact adversarial accuracy for the first time. R54 reduces BERT training from 3 days to 76 minutes. These are transformative, not incremental. Dense_low items like R01 (substantial but not transformative improvements) and R39 (1.6% accuracy gain) demonstrate smaller practical leaps.

proposals.name: Reusable Technique Generation
proposals.instruction: Score whether the core technique or analytical tool developed is likely to be independently useful beyond this paper's specific problem. 10 = introduces a general-purpose tool or analytical method that many future papers will adopt; 0 = the technique is narrowly tailored to one specific setting.
proposals.rationale: R16's exploration-preserving policy discretization and generalized G-optimal design are explicitly flagged as independently interesting. R23's coreset framework for robust clustering is reusable across algorithms. R55's bandit framework for integrating gradient priors is general. Dense_low items like R11 (order learning for age estimation) and R51 (binary DNN library) are more narrowly scoped.

proposals.name: Principle-Driven Component Coherence
proposals.instruction: Score whether all proposed components, modules, or design choices are derived from a single unifying principle, vs. being ad-hoc additions. 10 = every component follows naturally from one foundational principle or theory; 0 = multiple components with no shared theoretical justification.
proposals.rationale: R24 derives its entire architecture from ODE stability theory—anti-symmetry flows naturally from the principle. R46's redesign of the discriminator as a segmentation network follows from one idea. In contrast, R07 (dense_low) combines population-size encoding, hypernetworks, and multi-task training as three loosely connected components, which may explain the dense model's skepticism.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Explanation of Phenomena
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract provides a causal/mechanistic explanation for WHY a phenomenon occurs, rather than merely demonstrating THAT it occurs. 10 = identifies a specific, testable mechanism that explains the phenomenon; 0 = only shows empirical results without explaining the underlying cause.
proposals.rationale: R34 doesn't just show adversarial examples exist—it explains they arise from linearity, which also explains cross-architecture generalization. R52 uses influence functions and Hessian spectra to explain the mechanism behind double descent. R44 identifies two specific failure mechanisms for knowledge distillation on detection. Dense_low items like R05 report strong results without explaining why Transformers succeed as world models.

proposals.name: Domain-Independent Problem Formulation
proposals.instruction: Score whether the problem is formulated in terms general enough to apply across multiple application domains, vs. being tied to one specific application. 10 = fully domain-independent formulation applicable to many fields; 5 = formulated for a class of related problems; 0 = formulated only for one specific application.
proposals.rationale: R33's MIP formulation for piecewise-linear network verification applies to any such network. R48's higher-dimensional attention is motivated by but not limited to logical reasoning. R23's coreset framework applies to any robust clustering instance. Dense_low items like R11 (age estimation) and R30 (zebrafish classification) are domain-specific, which may limit perceived research significance.

proposals.name: Fundamental Trade-off Resolution
proposals.instruction: Score whether the paper resolves a well-known, fundamental tension or trade-off that the field has struggled with, rather than simply improving along one axis. 10 = resolves a deep, widely-recognized trade-off (e.g., stability vs. expressivity, exploration vs. exploitation); 0 = no tension is addressed.
proposals.rationale: R40 resolves the tension between opponent-shaping (LOLA's power) and convergence stability, proving SOS achieves both. R34 resolves the tension between the inter-architecture generality of adversarial examples and previous explanations. R24 resolves information propagation vs. training stability in deep graph networks. Dense_low items often optimize one axis without addressing a fundamental tension.

proposals.name: First-Principles Method Derivation
proposals.instruction: Score whether the proposed method is derived from foundational principles (axioms, physical laws, mathematical identities) rather than designed empirically or by intuition. 10 = complete derivation from first principles to practical method; 5 = partially principled with some empirical choices; 0 = pure empirical design with no theoretical derivation.
proposals.rationale: R15 derives its regularization from a loss expansion around quantization perturbation—purely first-principles. R18 derives fBNNs from the theorem that KL divergence between stochastic processes equals the supremum of marginal KL divergences. R54's LAMB is derived from a principled layerwise adaptation strategy. Dense_low items like R28 (amalgamation mechanisms designed empirically) and R37 (genetic operators chosen by analogy) lack this depth of derivation.

proposals.name: Prior-Work Framework Subsumption
proposals.instruction: Score whether the proposed framework mathematically subsumes multiple prior approaches as special cases or instances, demonstrating a deeper level of understanding. 10 = explicitly shows several prior methods are special cases of the new framework; 0 = treats prior work only as baselines to beat, without unifying relationship.
proposals.rationale: R60's generalized spherical CNN framework encompasses various existing approaches. R55's bandit framework conceptually unifies existing black-box attack methods and shows them to be optimal in a natural sense. R40's SOS interpolates between LOLA and LookAhead, subsuming both. Dense_low item R21 attempts unification of Lipschitz networks but the dense model may perceive the subsumption as retrospective rather than generative of new insight.

proposals.name: New Research Direction Opening
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work opens a new research direction that other researchers are likely to follow, creating new questions and opportunities. 10 = defines a new problem class or capability that spawns follow-up work; 0 = closes a small gap in an established area.
proposals.rationale: R26 opens the direction of training-time attacks on GNNs via meta-learning—a problem no one had studied. R48 opens higher-dimensional attention mechanisms for relational reasoning. R03 opens learned perturbation sets for robustness evaluation. Dense_low items like R49 (label encodings for regression) and R58 (ranking ensembles for HPO) refine existing directions rather than opening new ones.

proposals.name: Cross-Field Conceptual Bridge
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work forges a non-obvious, fruitful connection between two distinct research fields or mathematical traditions. 10 = a surprising and productive bridge between fields not previously connected; 5 = applies tools from one field to another in a straightforward way; 0 = works entirely within one established field.
proposals.rationale: R17 bridges differential geometry (curvature), probability (random walks), and optimal transport (Wasserstein distances) to define hypergraph curvature—a genuinely cross-field construct. R24 bridges ODE stability theory and graph neural networks. R42 bridges causal inference and NLP to clarify spurious correlations. Dense_low items like R56 (wavelets within texture synthesis) and R51 (binary networks within efficient inference) stay within their home fields.

proposals.name: Abstract verbosity
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the abstract is long and text-dense. Count total words and sentences. 0 = very short and sparse; 10 = very long and packed. Do not judge whether the length is good or bad.

proposals.name: Breadth-of-experiments signaling

proposals.name: Fundamental Assumption Challenged
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper completely overturns or deeply questions a core, widely-held assumption in the field (e.g., arguing a known problem is fundamentally misunderstood). Score 0 if it accepts all standard assumptions and merely optimizes within an existing paradigm.
proposals.rationale: The dense model appears to highly value paradigm-shifting perspectives that reframe how a problem is understood, which a rigid scorecard might miss if it only checks for standard solution components. R04 completely overturns the assumption that adversarial examples stem from nonlinearity; R50 provides a fundamental causal redefinition of 'spurious patterns'; R60 challenges the necessity of training the final classifier layer.

proposals.name: Provable Guarantees with Practical Algorithm
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract presents rigorous mathematical proofs or theoretical bounds AND provides an immediately usable, empirically validated algorithm. Score 0 if the work is purely informal or purely theoretical with no practical algorithmic realization.
proposals.rationale: The dense model heavily rewards the rare combination of deep theory immediately translated into a working, tested algorithm. R23 provides theoretical convergence proofs for SOS alongside strong empirical results; R24 formalizes verification as a mixed integer program while achieving massive computational speedups; R53 proves near-optimal bounds for robust clustering coresets and validates them empirically.

proposals.name: Elegance of Minimalist Solution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper solves a complex problem using a remarkably simple, minimalist approach or trivial modification that replaces prior complex heuristics. Score 0 if it relies on highly convoluted, multi-step, or heavily engineered architectures.
proposals.rationale: The dense model perceives conceptual elegance and simple fixes as high quality, whereas a scorecard might over-credit papers that bolt on many complex modules. R04 yields a simple and fast method of generating adversarial examples from a linear perspective; R60 fixes the classifier up to a global scale constant with little loss in accuracy; R51 achieves strong results with a simple linear learner.

proposals.name: Unified Formal Framework
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract introduces a single, elegant mathematical formulation that conceptually subsumes or generalizes multiple previously distinct or ad-hoc approaches. Score 0 if it proposes a standalone, highly specialized method that does not connect to existing frameworks.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards high-level unification of fragmented fields, a property hard for a discrete scorecard to capture. R22 introduces a 2-simplicial Transformer that generalizes dot-product attention; R24 unifies verification formulations via tight MIP constraints; R44 unifies training-time attacks by solving the bilevel problem via meta-gradients.

proposals.name: Order-of-Magnitude Practical Breakthrough
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract demonstrates an unprecedented, order-of-magnitude improvement (e.g., 10x to 100x faster) on a highly contested practical metric like training time, inference speed, or exactness. Score 0 if improvements are described as marginal or typical incremental gains.
proposals.rationale: The dense model recognizes that achieving massive practical leaps requires deep underlying insight, whereas a scorecard might only see 'an engineering paper'. R08 reduces BERT training time from 3 days to 76 minutes; R24 achieves a verifier that is two to three orders of magnitude quicker than the state-of-the-art.

proposals.name: Causal Mechanism for Observed Phenomena
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper provides a mechanistic, causal explanation for a widely observed empirical phenomenon, rather than just proposing a method that performs better. Score 0 if the work is entirely a black-box optimization or purely methodological without explaining why it works.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values 'why' things happen highly. R04 explains the most intriguing fact about adversarial examples (their cross-architecture generalization); R50 uses the language of causality to explain exactly why spurious associations form; R59 investigates the mechanisms behind double descent at the interpolation threshold.

proposals.name: Advanced Cross-Disciplinary Math Transfer
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper explicitly imports and adapts deep, formal mathematical machinery from a completely different domain (e.g., algebraic topology, quantum physics) to machine learning. Score 0 if it uses only standard, textbook machine learning mathematics.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard may over-credit exotic mathematics if the criteria simply count 'uses advanced math', while the dense model remains unimpressed if the math doesn't yield profound ML insights. R32 imports projective clustering from computational geometry for network compression; R46 utilizes generalized rectifier wavelet covariance models for texture synthesis; R55 imports hyperbolic uncertainty for self-paced learning.

proposals.name: Exhaustive Sub-Problem Configuration Mapping
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper systematically maps out and evaluates a vast array of configurations, hyperparameters, or architectural variants for a highly specific sub-problem. Score 0 if it evaluates only a single, monolithic proposed configuration.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard model with criteria like 'thorough ablation' might heavily reward narrow, exhaustive sweeps, while the dense model perceives this as a lack of fundamental contribution. R01 systematically defines and adapts to solution multiplicity; R28 exhaustively automates the space of label encodings for regression; R37 maps exactly when and where language-specific capacity matters across sub-layers.

proposals.name: Hybridization of Distinct Paradigms
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core framework is explicitly built by mechanically combining two or more independently popular, trendy modern paradigms (e.g., combining genetic algorithms with policy gradients). Score 0 if the method relies on a single, unified paradigm.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard might reward papers that 'check many boxes' by combining multiple trendy concepts, while the dense model penalizes them if the combination is unnatural. R05 hybridizes hypernetworks and mean-field games; R11 combines genetic algorithms (mutation/crossover) with imitation learning and policy gradients; R55 combines hyperbolic neural networks with self-paced learning.

proposals.name: Custom Systems-Level Engineering Solution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if custom, low-level systems, libraries, or hardware-specific algorithms are built from scratch to solve a specific efficiency bottleneck via heuristic engineering. Score 0 if the work is purely conceptual or relies on high-level algorithmic tweaking.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard may over-credit explicit 'systems-building' criteria, whereas the dense model might view pure engineering without algorithmic breakthroughs as lower research quality. R40 builds Espresso, a custom C/CUDA library for binary DNNs; R52 proposes Slalom, partitioning DNN computations for Trusted Execution Environments.

proposals.name: Novel Representation Format Transfer
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if an established representational format or encoding trick (e.g., coordinate neural fields, binary label encodings) is successfully transferred to a completely novel target or architecture. Score 0 if standard data representations are used without modification.
proposals.rationale: The dense model often under-weights clever but ultimately incremental format transfers that a scorecard might find novel. R28 automates the search for label encodings in regression; R41 applies coordinate-based neural representations (like NeRFs) to represent the weights of a pre-trained neural network.

proposals.name: Fine-Grained Sub-Component Routing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper proposes complex, fine-grained mechanisms for dynamically routing or mixing information between specific architectural sub-components (e.g., layers, image regions). Score 0 if it uses standard, monolithic end-to-end processing.
proposals.rationale: The dense model often penalizes papers that add architectural complexity without deep conceptual justification, whereas a scorecard might reward the nuanced 'mechanism'. R17 introduces a learnable downsampling module to selectively sample difficult locations; R26 devises cross-layer attention to retrieve information from previous layers; R37 schedules language-specific capacity across sub-layers.

proposals.name: Rigorous Application to Specialized Domain
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if standard deep learning techniques are carefully applied to a highly specific, non-standard real-world domain (e.g., biology, specific physics simulations) with rigorous domain-specific evaluation. Score 0 for pure theory or standard ML benchmarks (like CIFAR-10).
proposals.rationale: A scorecard might reward the immediate real-world applicability to a niche problem, while the dense model discounts papers that apply existing methods rather than introducing fundamental ML innovations. R35 applies CNNs to zebrafish swim bout classification; R56 applies order learning specifically to facial age estimation.

proposals.name: Domain-Agnostic Theoretical Generalizability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core method or theory is completely independent of any specific data modality or narrow architecture, applying abstractly to any model. Score 0 if the method is highly tailored to a specific modality (e.g., only vision or only text).
proposals.rationale: The dense model values fundamental, abstract properties of learning that span all of AI, which may be missed by a scorecard drawn to specific benchmark numbers. R18 frames adversarial defense as a modality-agnostic minimax game; R23 proposes stable opponent shaping for all differentiable games; R24 applies to piecewise-linear networks universally.

proposals.name: Algorithmic Formulation of Intuitive Heuristics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a formal, algorithmic framework replaces or models what was previously an intuitive, manual, or ad-hoc heuristic used by practitioners. Score 0 if no prior heuristic is formalized into an algorithm.
proposals.rationale: The dense model recognizes that mathematically capturing practitioner intuition is a strong indicator of research quality. R19 uses determinantal point processes to algorithmically determine the intuitive trade-off in data compression quality; R53 adapts a framework for capacity-constrained clustering to handle outlier points algorithmically.

proposals.name: Explicit Code Repository Links
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (absent) to 10 (highly prominent) the extent to which the abstract contains an explicit URL to a code repository (e.g., GitHub) or explicitly states that code is open-sourced. Do not judge the quality or usefulness of the code, only the presence of the repository mention.
proposals.rationale: The inclusion of explicit GitHub links is a surface formatting choice heavily concentrated in specific rows (e.g., R01, R20, R44). It acts as a proxy for an author's open-source norms or institutional PR practices rather than the core textual quality itself.

proposals.name: Density of Inline Math Notation
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text contains raw inline mathematical notation and symbols (e.g., $\mathbb{R}$, $k$-Means, $\epsilon$-coreset). 0 means no math symbols, 10 means heavily interspersed with them. Do not judge if the math is correct, elegant, or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Typographical density like inline LaTeX commands (visible in R09 and R22) is a surface-level formatting habit. It may correlate with theoretical subfields but is not itself an indicator of the underlying research quality.

proposals.name: Named Benchmark and Model Drops
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 the extent to which the abstract explicitly drops the names of well-known datasets, hardware, or models (e.g., BERT, ImageNet, Atari, TPU, ResNet) as a primary feature of its validation. Do not judge whether the benchmark is appropriate or the results are good.
proposals.rationale: Name-dropping major benchmarks and models (prominent in R01 and R20) is often a fingerprint of well-resourced labs or institutional PR practices designed to trigger keyword matches, serving as a proxy for reputation rather than intrinsic quality.

proposals.name: Explicit Template Boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the abstract includes verbatim conference template phrases (e.g., 'One-sentence Summary', 'Code Of Ethics', 'Broader Impacts'). Do not judge whether the inclusion of this boilerplate is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Explicit template adherence text (such as the 'Code Of Ethics' and 'One-sentence Summary' in R07) is a pure formatting artifact left by filling out specific venue submission templates, completely orthogonal to the research quality.

proposals.name: Playful or Pun-based Title
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 the extent to which the title contains a pun, a pop-culture reference, or a conversational question. 0 means strictly descriptive, 10 means heavily reliant on wordplay. Do not judge if the title is catchy or clever.
proposals.rationale: Conversational or pun-based titles (e.g., 'A Very Good Method...' in R38, 'Kill two birds by one stone' in R04) often indicate a late-arriving, highly networked author riding community trend cycles, acting as a stylistic tell rather than a measure of quality.

proposals.name: Explicit Hardware Scale Mentions
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 the extent to which the abstract highlights specific hardware infrastructure or computational scale (e.g., mentioning TPUs, massive parallelization, or exact GPU hours). Do not judge the value or impressiveness of the scale.
proposals.rationale: Mentioning massive computational hardware (visible in R06 and R20) is a textual fingerprint of well-funded labs. It predicts reception by signaling resource abundance rather than reflecting the underlying intellectual merit of the idea.

proposals.name: Explicit Contribution Enumeration
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 the extent to which the text uses explicit, numbered list phrasing to introduce its own contributions (e.g., 'Our contributions are three-fold', 'First... Second...'). Do not judge whether the contributions are clear or valid.
proposals.rationale: Rigid enumeration of contributions (as seen in R18 and R07) is a stylistic fingerprint left by heavy copyediting or coaching on academic writing norms, predicting a well-resourced submission pipeline rather than the raw quality of the research.

proposals.name: Explicit Prior Author Citations
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 the extent to which specific previous authors or research groups are named directly in the prose (e.g., 'Kipf and Welling', 'Semmelhack et al.'). Do not judge the relevance of the citation.
proposals.rationale: Naming specific authors in the abstract text (such as in R44 and R56) leaves a fingerprint of the author's seniority and network position. It reflects the author's embeddedness in the field's lineage, which predicts reception but is not a quality metric itself.

proposals.name: SOTA Acronym Usage
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 the extent to which the abstract explicitly uses the acronym 'SOTA' or the exact phrase 'state-of-the-art'. Do not judge whether the paper actually achieves state-of-the-art results.
proposals.rationale: The use of the SOTA acronym or state-of-the-art phrasing (present in R14 and R25) is a community style marker reflecting a hyper-competitive subculture. It is a self-promotional textual habit rather than an objective indicator of research value.

proposals.name: Niche Application Domain Focus
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 the extent to which the abstract frames the research explicitly around a highly specific non-ML application domain (e.g., specific biological organisms, driving systems). Do not judge the importance or validity of the application.
proposals.rationale: Framing the paper around a niche application (like 'zebrafish' in R56 or 'autonomous driving' in R14) indicates the paper originates from a specific applied upstream field. This domain-targeting mechanism acts as a proxy for audience overlap rather than ML research quality.
